portion_doctrine: Segments 11-20 cover three major topics: (1) Photography contracts for headshots, portraits, and wedding videography with detailed clause structures and non-refundable deposit policies; (2) Copyright/licensing fundamentals showing photographers own IP by default, clients pay for licenses not ownership, and detailed licensing structures; (3) Licensing fee pricing models using three criteria (use case, term, region, exclusivity) with real-world examples from resort/brand photographers.
operating_rules: Non-refundable deposit clause: reserve time and deposits are non-refundable even if portrait rescheduled/canceled except for inclement weather
Photographer can reschedule if weather/lighting conditions prevent portrait meeting artistic standards
Act of God clause: fire, casualties, strike, illness means photographer returns deposit but has no further liability
Copyright ownership: photographer retains copyright even after full payment unless explicitly transferred in writing
Client cannot modify, crop, edit, or post photos without photographer attribution and written consent
Exclusivity in wedding videography: photographer is sole hired videographer for video services (photography by others allowed)
License cancellation policy: if client cancels/no-shows, photographer keeps payment unless photographer rebooks that slot
Artistic release: dissatisfaction with aesthetic/creative judgment not valid reason to terminate or request refund
Three-component pricing structure for commercial work: (1) Production expenses (crew/travel/permits/gear/props), (2) Creative fee (day rate/profit margin), (3) Rights/usage fee (licensing)
Default copyright ownership: photographer owns copyright to all created images unless explicitly transferred
Use case licensing determines rights: organic social, paid social, website, web ads, display ads, billboards, print each priced differently
Term (duration) licensing: charge more for perpetuity than limited terms (1 month to 5 years), discount for longer durations
Regional licensing: local (city/county) lowest cost, national/US higher, worldwide highest; varies by market size/buying power
Exclusivity premium: charge significantly more if brand cannot re-license to competitors/other companies
Two-company rule: if single person owns two separate businesses (two tax filings), each needs separate license fee
Product company usage: flooring companies, furniture makers, material suppliers need separate license to use photos in lookbooks/marketing
Perpetuity licensing costs more: brands wanting forever usage must understand and accept higher fees than annual licenses
License fee strategy for small brands: bundle into single fee and don't itemize separately; for large brands itemize separately in contract
prompts: When client wants to use photos commercially: ask three questions - (1) Where will it be used? (2) For how long? (3) In what region?
For wedding contracts: require additional contact person who is not bride/groom but has authority (parent/planner/coordinator)
During sales call: coach clients on where content will live - website, YouTube ads, TikTok ads, etc. to determine license type
tools: HoneyBook: client management software with contract templates and auto-payment processing (50% discount first year via affiliate)
The Law Tog: photography-specific contract templates by lawyer/photographer
PhotoQuote Pro: pricing calculator for licensing fees based on use case/term/region/exclusivity (no subscription, updated by real photographers)
gates: Never send a licensing price quote before understanding all usage terms (use case, term, region, exclusivity)
Contract validation: date, client/photographer details, services description, pricing, deposit amount and date, delivery timeframe
content_ideas: Licensing as revenue multiplier: $2K shoot can become multiple five-figure deal with proper licensing
Single shoot monetization: $40K from 3-day shoot via licensing to Fortune 500 brands (Marriott, Molokai, Sandals)
Travel photographer licensing: $5K single deal from tourism boards for existing photos already taken
Event-to-licensing: photos taken at architecture event can be licensed to architecture firms for marketing
contradictions: TENSION: Small brands don't want to pay licensing fees separately but large brands expect itemized breakdown - RESOLUTION: bundle for small, itemize for large
TENSION: Photographer gave discount to new interior design client hoping for future work - zero future projects resulted; giving work free sets wrong tone for relationship
weird_gold: Elevator slideshow discovery: four-seasons guest saw own photos playing in hotel elevator as part of digital license - unexpected use case that validates broad licensing

Hembree/Apple precedent: band that sold Holy Water song for downloads later licensed same song to Apple for Super Bowl ad at much higher rate - music licensing proves double-dipping is standard business practice
Shop-lifting analogy: even though photos are easy to screenshot/email/save-as, ease of theft doesn't make unauthorized use legal - just like leaving car unlocked doesn't make stealing it legal
